hints.junior: Nothing was ever actually saved — the project list was held in a JS variable for as long as the tab happened to stay open, and a reload wipes that clean.
hints.mid: A reload doesn't reset in-memory state, it destroys the JS context entirely. The only path back to data is the network, with no fallback if that fails.
hints.staff: Keeping a value in memory, persisting it across loads, and supporting real offline use are three different things — IndexedDB is the only one of the three that does the last two.

hints.junior: Load projects, then try Simulate reload with Go offline both off and on, in each mode, and watch what the list does.
hints.mid: Broken mode always empties the list on reload and has to refetch. Fixed mode reads the same data back from a real IndexedDB object store, instantly.
hints.staff: The fixed mode calls real indexedDB.open/put/getAll — check DevTools' Application → IndexedDB panel while it runs to watch the store fill in live.

hints.junior: IndexedDB stores real JS objects, not just strings, and every read/write is async — you listen for success or error instead of getting a value back immediately.
hints.mid: open() → onupgradeneeded creates stores → transaction().objectStore().put()/getAll(), each a request with its own success/error handler.
hints.staff: A transaction auto-commits once it has no pending requests queued — await unrelated work inside one and the next request throws TransactionInactiveError.

hints.junior: More code than a plain variable, worth it when losing data on reload genuinely hurts — not worth it for data that's cheap and fast to refetch.
hints.mid: idb (a small promise wrapper) removes most of the callback ceremony without changing the transaction rules — worth it past one or two call sites.
hints.staff: Read-cache-first-then-revalidate is the same stale-while-revalidate idea SWR/React Query apply to network responses, just backed by disk instead of an in-memory query cache.

sections.junior: Today's case is about a project list that only ever lived in a JS variable — it looked fine in every demo, but a reload or a dead connection wiped it clean with no way back.
sections.mid: In-memory state only exists for the lifetime of the current JS runtime — a reload destroys that context entirely, and if the network's down when it tries to refetch, there's nothing to fall back on.
sections.staff: The real gap is between keeping a value in memory, persisting it across page loads, and actually supporting offline use — those are three different guarantees, and only IndexedDB delivers the last two.

sections.junior: IndexedDB stores real objects, not just strings, inside named object stores, and every read and write is asynchronous instead of instant like local storage.
sections.mid: You open the database, create your stores in the upgrade hook, then read and write through transactions, each operation returning a request you attach handlers to.
sections.staff: The sharp edge is transaction lifetime — a transaction commits itself the moment it has no pending requests, so awaiting something unrelated inside one and then trying to use it again throws an error.

sections.junior: Load the projects, then try reloading with the network on and with it switched off, in each mode, and watch whether the list survives.
sections.mid: Broken mode starts from nothing on every reload and depends entirely on the network. Fixed mode reads the same data straight back out of a real IndexedDB store first.
sections.staff: Every write and read in fixed mode here is a genuine indexedDB call — open DevTools and watch the actual object store fill in as you click through it.

sections.junior: A JS variable is not a cache. If losing the data on reload would actually hurt, IndexedDB is what persists it and keeps working offline.
sections.mid: Write every successful fetch into an IndexedDB read model, read from it first on load, then revalidate over the network in the background.
sections.staff: Keep async work outside the transaction boundary, and only reach for this where losing data on reload has a real cost — cheap-to-refetch data doesn't need it.
